opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a big question, and I think the honest answer is that the change will be both more gradual and more profound than people expect.

In the near term, I think the biggest impact will be in the less glamorous parts of healthcare: documentation, scheduling, triage, and summarizing the huge amount of data that piles up in a patient's record. Clinicians spend an enormous share of their day on paperwork, and if AI can take some of that off their plates, that's time back with patients. That may not make headlines, but it matters a great deal for burnout and for quality of care.

Further out, I'm most excited about imaging and precision medicine. My own work has focused a lot on using medical images, CT scans in particular, to predict how a patient's cancer might behave or respond to treatment. There's information in those images that the human eye simply can't pick up, and machine learning lets us extract it. Over the next decade I think we'll see more of these tools move from research papers into actual clinical decision-making, helping oncologists choose the right therapy for the right patient earlier.

That said, I want to be careful not to oversell it. The hard problems aren't really the algorithms anymore. They're data quality, bias, privacy, and integration into clinical workflows. A model trained at one hospital often doesn't generalize to another, and if our training data underrepresents certain populations, we risk building tools that widen health disparities instead of closing them. So a lot of the next ten years has to be about validation, regulation, and building trust with both clinicians and patients.

Ultimately I don't see AI replacing doctors. I see it as giving them better instruments, the way imaging itself did decades ago. The clinicians who use AI well will likely deliver better care than those who don't, and I think that's the real shift we're heading toward.

r001.rationale: The response describes potential benefits for patients and the need to build trust, but does not say that tangible patient benefits will drive acceptance of AI.

r002.rationale: It predicts future clinical use of AI tools but does not suggest existing tools may already be sufficient to make a meaningful difference for patients.

r003.rationale: The response does not credit large language models with bringing AI into clinical settings.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the biggest changes over the next ten years won't be the ones that make headlines. Everyone imagines an AI that diagnoses cancer from a scan better than a radiologist, and some of that will happen, but the real transformation is going to be quieter and more structural.

Right now, a huge amount of what a clinician does is not clinical. It's documentation, it's searching through fragmented records, it's reconciling medication lists, it's waiting on results that got lost somewhere between departments. I think within a decade, a lot of that friction disappears. The ambient listening tools that write the note while the doctor talks to the patient are already here, and they're going to get much better. That alone gives people back time, and time is the scarcest resource in healthcare.

The second thing I'd point to is that we'll stop thinking about AI as a single model that gives you an answer, and start thinking about it as something that follows the patient through their whole journey. In my own work in surgical oncology, the interesting questions aren't just "is this a tumor" but "how will this patient recover, what complications are they at risk for, should we operate at all." Those are longitudinal problems. They need data from imaging, from the lab, from the operating room, from what happens after discharge. Ten years from now I expect we'll have systems that actually integrate those streams, rather than tools that each solve one narrow task in isolation.

What I'm more cautious about is the gap between what we can build and what actually gets deployed safely. We're very good at publishing papers where a model does well on a benchmark. We're much worse at validating these things across different hospitals, different populations, different scanners. A model trained in one centre can quietly fall apart somewhere else. So I'd say a lot of the next decade is really going to be about the unglamorous work of evaluation, monitoring, and figuring out who is accountable when the system gets something wrong.

And finally, I think the role of the clinician changes but doesn't go away. The best framing I've heard is that AI won't replace doctors, but doctors who use it well will have a very different job than doctors who don't. The judgment, the conversation with the patient, the decision about what matters to this person in front of you, that stays human. What changes is how much of the machinery underneath gets handled for them.

r002.rationale: It says ambient listening tools are already available, but does not suggest current tools are already sufficient to make a meaningful difference for patients.

astra-6.text:
I think over the next ten years, we’ll see AI become more integrated into everyday healthcare—helping clinicians interpret images, identify risks earlier, and make better use of the information they already collect. There’s also an opportunity to reduce the administrative burden, giving healthcare teams more time with patients.

But the real measure of progress will be whether these tools improve patient outcomes. Can they work reliably across different hospitals and patient populations? Can clinicians understand when to trust them and when to question them? That will require careful validation and close collaboration with patients and healthcare professionals. I see AI supporting clinical judgment, with people remaining central to care.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see AI become much more integrated into everyday care, helping clinicians make sense of the enormous amount of information they already collect. That could mean spotting disease earlier, identifying which patients need closer monitoring, or helping tailor treatment to an individual.

But the biggest challenge is turning a promising model into something that actually improves care. We need to know that it works across different patient populations, fits into clinical workflows, and gives clinicians information they can act on. Over the next ten years, I’d like to see success measured less by how impressive an algorithm looks and more by whether patients have better outcomes and better access to care.

r001.rationale: The response says AI success should be measured by better patient outcomes and access, but does not predict that tangible benefits will drive acceptance of AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses potential future uses and the challenge of turning models into improved care; it does not suggest existing AI tools are already sufficient to make a meaningful difference.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention large language models or credit them with bringing AI into clinical settings.
